scope: Second review of the 318 task packages added from autoresearch-tasks commit 374288ac83ee35dc6b08b5ce2484f2af208c7e07, made after a maintainer reported missing and incorrect evaluators, and a review of the evaluators of the 1,301 instance-level open-problem packages added in the same pull request.
method: Ten auditors, one per group of packages. For every package the evaluator was compared with the cited paper and, where one exists, with the benchmark's official or widely used public implementation; an independent implementation written from the definition was compared with the library on the seed, on reference objects from the literature and on random valid, invalid and hostile inputs; the seed was run. A defect was fixed only after it had been demonstrated, and every fix has a regression test in tasks/tests/test_audit_*.py. Statement changes were applied to every copy of a statement and checked for consistency. The open-problem packages were swept mechanically and their thirteen verifier modules were audited in the same way.

mcts-ahd-asp-constructive.compared_with: Pinned upstream evaluator problems/asp_constructive/eval.py of zz1358m/MCTS-AHD-master at commit ee9c4f4 (read, not run); MCTS-AHD, arXiv 2501.08603, Appendix B.1 and F.1 (Table 7); FunSearch repository, admissible_set/admissible_set.ipynb.
checks: Not run: no checkout exists here and this audit does not execute downloaded code. run.py evaluate answers 'Run setup for this task first', which is truthful.

Upstream eval.py at the pinned commit imports logging, copy, itertools, math, sys, os.path and numpy only; train mode evaluates n=15, w=10 and returns the size of the expanded set; no check of the final set (as the statement says).

The local adapter (tasks/adapters/recovered/optimization_original.py) imports torch inside try/except ImportError and calls evaluator.evaluate(15, 10) once, so PyTorch and SciPy are not needed for this problem; max_instances, iterations and ants are not used.

What is needed to run it: network access to github.com and git for 'python3 run.py setup mcts-ahd-asp-constructive' (shallow fetch of the pinned commit into the task cache; the runner checks the commit of the checkout), and NumPy. Nothing has to be installed on this machine besides the checkout.
The seed (priority_v1 returning 1) is the trivial priority; FunSearch's notebook states that it builds 1842 vectors, the value recorded for the seed in task.json.
No other package of the suite uses this adapter; the nine other tasks of the same paper are recreated NumPy tasks labelled 'method'.

open item settled: a 15-colour colouring of K16 exists. Of the 631 starters of Z_15, 96 give a one-factorisation of K16 (translates of the starter, each with the pair {inf, i}) in which no two factors contain a four-cycle; the checker accepts the first with score 15 and my own count finds five colours on every K4 (eg16_starters.py, eg16_15.json; regression test)

the usual n-1 colour colouring ({i,j} -> i+j mod 15, {inf,i} -> 2i mod 15, the patterned starter) has exactly five K4s {inf,a,a+5,a+10} with three colours and is rejected; a 16-colour colouring found by local search is accepted with score 16

findings.what: The stated range 13 <= f(16) <= 15 is true, but not for the stated reason, and its lower end is not the best known. The upper bound 15 does not follow from a general inequality f(n) < n: the published n-1 colour constructions need n-1 prime (Erdős and Gyárfás) or n not congruent to 1 modulo 3 (Krop and Krop), and 16 is neither. It holds because a 15-colour colouring exists (found here in under a second). The lower bound is 14 by f(n) >= 5(n-1)/6 + 1. So the first review's suspicion that the range might be 13 to 16 does not apply; the range is 14 to 15.

findings.what: Open item of the first review: the limitation says two-dimensional toroidal instances are polynomially solvable in principle (Barahona 1982) and that a candidate implementing such an algorithm should reach the optimum. Read against the sources: polynomial solvability by matching holds for planar lattices; for the torus the known polynomial algorithms (Pfaffian enumeration of the cut generating function) require integer couplings bounded by a polynomial in the lattice size. The couplings here are integers up to 375001, so that route is pseudo-polynomial and the sentence overstates what a candidate can implement within the budget.
findings.fix: statement: limitations[1] and sources[1].locator

findings.what: The statement attributes the optimal values to branch-and-cut runs of Liers et al.; the library documentation only says that the tables list 'the optimal solution values' and credits the instances to Frauke Liers. The values themselves are right: the three 10x10 optima were recomputed exactly and all 18 equal Table 10.
findings.fix: none: attribution detail, not used in judging

statement_changes.old: Two-dimensional toroidal instances are polynomially solvable in principle (Barahona 1982); a candidate that implements such an algorithm should reach the optimum, which is the intended research content of this task.
statement_changes.new: Planar two-dimensional lattices without a field are polynomially solvable by matching (Barahona 1982), but these instances are toroidal: for graphs on the torus, polynomial algorithms are known when the integer couplings are bounded by a polynomial in the lattice size (Pfaffian enumeration; Galluccio, Loebl and Vondrak 2001, who credit Barahona 1982 for toroidal square lattices). The couplings here are integers up to about 3.8e5, so that method is pseudo-polynomial for these instances. A transfer-matrix dynamic programme over rows solves the three 10x10 instances exactly in seconds and confirms their published optima; it does not scale to 15x15 and 20x20 within the budget, where the task is a test of heuristics.
statement_changes.reason: The cited result does not give a practical polynomial algorithm for toroidal instances with large weights.
statement_changes.evidence: doi:10.1007/PL00011425 (abstract) and its preprint kam.mff.cuni.cz/kamserie/clanky/1999/s443.pdf (introduction); doi:10.1088/0305-4470/15/10/028 (abstract); audit run an independent check exact0..2 (10x10 optima 6049461, 5757868, 6509837 in 11 s each).

miplib.reference: MIPLIB 2017 (Gleixner et al. 2021), open instances: https://miplib.zib.de/tag_open.html. checks: Official rule read from the source: a bound may be violated by tol * max(1, |bound|, |x|); a row by tol * max(1, positive part of the activity, |side|); integrality by tol (absolute); an indicator row binds when its binary is on the trigger side of 1/2; all in exact rational arithmetic. The task's rule (1e-6 absolute everywhere, in floating point) is contained in it, so nothing accepted here is rejected there.

findings.what: The feasibility rule is stricter than MIPLIB's own: 1e-6 absolute against tol * max(1, scale) with tol = 1e-5 (checker default) or 1e-4 (MIPLIB's run scripts). It is stated in the checker's source, quoted in the reference above.

dnacode.reference: O. D. King, Bounds for DNA codes with constant GC-content, Electron. J. Combin. 10 (2003) R33 (definitions of A4GC(n,d,w) and A4GC,RC(n,d,w): H(x, y) >= d for distinct codewords and H(x, y^RC) >= d for all, not necessarily distinct, codewords; tables for w = n/2), https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v10i1r33; Chee and Ling, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 54 (2008) 391-394, arXiv:0803.3657 (tables for w = floor(n/2)); table page of Gaborit and King, https://rambutan.umassmed.edu/king/dnacodes.html (last updated 23 June 2010). Independent implementations: pure-Python definition and an exact branch-and-bound clique search, scratch checks/fuzz_exact.py, checks/dnacode_exact.py, checks/dnacode_replay.py.
checks: 4,000 random word sets (n = 2..8, with and without the reverse-complement rule; 2,506 valid): accept/reject and size equal to the pure-Python definition.

Exact maximum codes by clique search for A4GC(4,3), (4,4), (5,4), (5,5) and A4GC,RC(4,3), (4,4), (5,4), (5,5), for every GC-weight w: the maxima at w = floor(n/2) are 12, 4, 10, 3 and 6, 2, 3, 1, the optimal entries of the table, and no other w gives more; each optimal code is accepted by the library. This confirms the verifier's reading of the constraints (complement A-T, C-G; reverse complement applied to all pairs including a word with itself).

findings.what: All 130 packages say 'The tables list the maximum over the GC-content w'. The tables are for w = floor(n/2): King 2003 gives his tables 'for these same parameters' as the earlier ones, 'n <= 12 (n even) with d <= n and w = n/2', and Chee and Ling 2008 describe the Gaborit-King table as 'the best available lower bounds on A4GC,RC(n, d, floor(n/2)), the size of DNA codes having 50% GC-content'. The task (any one constant w) is a relaxation of the tabulated problem: every record stays valid for the task, but a larger code with another w would improve the task's record and not the table entry, which the statement should say. The same sentence is in the docstring of arnew/dnacode.py.

matbench.reference: Matbench v0.1 (Dunn et al. 2020): official folds in matbench_v0.1_validation.json of materialsproject/matbench (pinned commit 936176db), mean over the five folds of the test MAE (regression) or of the ROC AUC of the predicted labels, which matbench computes from labels and which equals the balanced accuracy (classification). Leaderboards: https://matbench.materialsproject.org/ (per-task pages). The scorer is autoresearch_suite.chem_matbench (shared, read only). Independent check: scratch checks/matbench_folds.py.
checks: glass prepared on 2026-11-24 (46 MB for the validation file): the derived task file is byte-identical to the origin's; its five test folds equal the official test ids and the complements equal the official train ids; the targets equal the raw gfa column. The official classification folds are those of StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle, random_state 18012019), not of KFold, as an independent split shows.

snake.reference: Snake-in-the-box: longest induced path in the hypercube Q_n (Kautz 1958); length = number of edges. Record source: T. Ace, Snake-in-the-Box lower bounds, https://www.minortriad.com/snake/ (leaderboard with one transition sequence per record). Independent implementation: pairwise Hamming-distance definition, scratch checks/fuzz_exact.py and checks/snake_live.py.
checks: 3,000 random walks in Q_2..Q_6 (induced and not): accept/reject and length equal to the pairwise definition.

The four record snakes of the live leaderboard (fetched 2026-11-24) replayed from their transition sequences: 379, 750, 1480 and 2946 edges in dimensions 10..13, accepted by the library and by the independent check, equal to the package records; a corrupted copy of each is rejected.
Hostile inputs: duplicates, out-of-range and negative vertices, closed cycle, chord, single vertex, nested lists, NaN rejected.
Seeds through run.py: 145, 232, 585, 1017 for dimensions 10..13; valid, equal to the origin's records.
